title: Louis Armstrong's 1965 return to New Orleans
summary: Tex says he put Armstrong's arrival on the air in 1965, disputes that black press was shut out, and mentions Al Corbetti and changing race relations.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: I get you. You were involved, you were working at the weekly when Louis Armstrong came back in 65. When he made his...
Yeah, I was writing a collier man. Yeah.
Yeah. Now, did you cover Louis when he came back in 65?

Did you cover that? I didn't officially cover Louis as such, but we got together and owned a couple of affairs and we had a couple of social visits, but I didn't do the writing or did the covering at that time. Other people were doing things because I was doing some other things. And if I, in 65, I'll tell you what I did do. I put his coming to New Orleans on the air because I was doing a newscasting. I might have a tape on it also because I used to tape a lot of my programs on Louis Armstrong. In fact, I said, ladies and gentlemen, went to the New Orleans airport and here comes the world's greatest ambassador, Louis Armstrong, once again in New Orleans and blah, blah, blah, whatever I had to say about it. I put it on the air. It didn't cover nothing in the newspaper.
My question was is that I've read, I don't know, wasn't it in the weekly that the black press kind of got shut out of coverage, that they had problems getting access to Louis when he came back
in the weekly, somewhere, maybe it was. Well,
that may have been an individual's definition of him or her who was trying to get to Louis. You see, they, you know,

Yeah, yeah. You see, you gotta remember, in 1965, when Louis came in, any pictures you saw in the Louisiana Weekly or in the Times-Picayune, you saw my face in my head right there with Louis Armstrong. Yeah,
yeah. And even in the museum.

And even in his book, my pictures right there with him. Yeah. And, you know, because I talk with Al Corbetti, who is a very, very good friend, who was partly raised with Louis Armstrong. In fact, Al is one of the gentlemen who is building, putting that structure. I think I, did I show you a copy of that? Yeah, letter. Yeah. That they're doing this. They've done more, in a sense, in New York for Louis Armstrong than we're doing here in New Orleans. Of course, I can understand the reason why. Because New York was way ahead of us. But in the South, we still have our racial concerns and problems. It was just within the last 12 or 15 years that you could be buried out at Lake Lawn. It's been the last 15, 20 years that white funeral fallers would embalm black people that wouldn't touch us years ago. Things have actually changed. But then again, you got a new thing happening on the scene. You got whites and blacks marrying now. Sure. You know, I got it in my family now, you know. Oh. And my grandson is married to a Caucasian now, you know. And I'm the grandfather, the great-grandfather of a, well, let me know, I'm a Caucasian child. Yes, I am. But it's still my grandchild.
